extra.message: byReference() builds a native SQL query by directly concatenating the caller-supplied 'reference' string into the SQL text: em.createNativeQuery("select * from application_record where reference = '"+reference+"'",...). The value originates from ApiController.byRef(@PathVariable String reference) (GET /api/applications/by-reference/{reference}), reachable by compliance_officer/bank_admin roles. An attacker-controlled reference such as ' OR '1'='1 or a UNION-based payload breaks out of the string literal, allowing arbitrary SQL injection against the application database.

packet() builds a shell command with new ProcessBuilder("sh","-c","soffice --headless --convert-to pdf "+label+" --outdir "+packetDir) where label is an unsanitized @RequestParam String from POST /api/applications/{id}/packet. Because the command is run through "sh -c", shell metacharacters in label (e.g. ; touch pwned; rm -rf / or $( ... )) are interpreted by the shell, giving an onboarding_officer-authenticated attacker arbitrary OS command execution.

restore() feeds the fully attacker-controlled 'legacy_state' cookie straight into new ObjectInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(Base64.getDecoder().decode(state))).readObject(). /legacy/** is permitAll() in SecurityConfig, so this is reachable pre-authentication. Native Java deserialization of untrusted bytes is a classic remote code execution vector when any gadget-chain-capable class (commons-collections, etc.) is on the classpath.

resume() parses the 'assertion' request parameter with com.nimbusds.jwt.SignedJWT.parse(assertion) and immediately trusts parsed.getJWTClaimsSet().getSubject() to look up the acting user via auth.require(subject) -- the signature is never verified (no JWSVerifier/verify() call). Combined with /legacy/** being permitAll(), any unauthenticated caller can submit a trivially-forged, unsigned-looking JWT with an arbitrary 'sub' claim and impersonate any user to read their application status.

cwe: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature

extra.message: importRequirements() builds a JsonMapper with activateDefaultTyping(LaissezFaireSubTypeValidator.instance, DefaultTyping.NON_FINAL, JsonTypeInfo.As.PROPERTY) and then calls typed.readValue(rules, Object.class) on the caller-supplied 'rules' @RequestParam string. LaissezFaireSubTypeValidator imposes no restriction on which classes may be instantiated, so an attacker (any bank_admin-authenticated caller, or anyone who can reach this with a forged/stolen token) can supply a @class-tagged JSON payload that instantiates arbitrary classes on the classpath -- a well-known Jackson polymorphic-deserialization RCE gadget vector.

projection() takes 'calcRule' straight from the attacker-controlled 'calc_rule' cookie (@CookieValue(defaultValue="annualIncome * 0.9")) and passes it unmodified to a BeanShell ScriptEngine's engine.eval(calcRule, ...). BeanShell scripts can call arbitrary Java (e.g. Runtime.getRuntime().exec(...)), so an attacker who sets a malicious calc_rule cookie achieves full remote code execution in the onboarding-officer/compliance-officer authenticated context.

requirementNotice() builds the FreeMarker template SOURCE by string-concatenating the @PathVariable 'section' directly into the template text (new Template("notice", "...the "+section+" check...", cfg)) and then processes it. Because 'section' becomes part of the template body rather than a data value, an attacker can supply FreeMarker directives/interpolations (e.g. ${"freemarker.template.utility.Execute"?new()("id")}) in the URL path segment to achieve server-side template injection and remote code execution.

campaign() opens an outbound HTTP connection to the caller-supplied CampaignCreate.callbackUrl with no allow-list, scheme check, or private-IP/metadata-endpoint block: HttpURLConnection conn=(HttpURLConnection)URI.create(b.callbackUrl).toURL().openConnection(). A compliance_officer-authenticated caller can point callbackUrl at internal-only services (e.g. core-mock, cloud metadata IPs) and have the onboarding-api server make the request on their behalf, including campaign/segment data in the POST body.

directory() builds the LDAP search filter by concatenating the @PathVariable 'account' straight into the query: ctx.search(DIRECTORY_BASE_DN,"(&(objectClass=person)(uid="+account+"))",controls). An attacker-controlled account value such as *)(uid=*))(|(uid=* breaks out of the intended filter, enabling LDAP filter injection to alter search logic or exfiltrate unintended directory attributes.

referenceMatch() extracts 'requestedReference' from an uploaded XML file's criteria/@ref attribute (fully attacker-controlled) and concatenates it directly into an XPath expression: String expr="//application[reference='"+requestedReference+"']"; then evaluates it with XPathFactory. A crafted ref value such as '] | //application[1]/.. | //*[' lets an uploader break out of the intended predicate and alter the query to return arbitrary application records across branches.

archive() resolves the attacker-controlled 'X-Report-Name' header directly against the packet directory with no sanitization or containment check: Path dest=dir.resolve(reportName);Files.write(dest,...). Unlike FileStore (which validates target.startsWith(base)), there is no normalize()/startsWith() guard here, so a reportName of ../../../../etc/cron.d/evil or an absolute path lets an onboarding_officer-authenticated caller write a file anywhere the process has permissions.

packetFile() resolves the attacker-controlled 'ref' @RequestParam directly against packetDir with no normalize()/startsWith() containment check before reading it: Path target=Path.of(packetDir).resolve(ref); ... Files.newInputStream(target). A ref value such as ../../../../etc/passwd lets any onboarding_officer/compliance_officer/bank_admin-authenticated caller read arbitrary files on the server's filesystem.

print() builds an HTML page by directly concatenating application fields (reference, address, employmentStatus) into the response body with zero HTML-escaping, then returns it as TEXT_HTML via @ResponseBody. 'address' is attacker-controllable free text (up to 500 chars, set via POST /api/applications/{id}/steps/address_details during onboarding). An applicant can store an XSS payload like <script>...</script> in their own address field; when any staff member later opens /applications/{id}/print, the script executes in the staff member's authenticated session (stored XSS).

download() is annotated @CrossOrigin(originPatterns="*",allowCredentials="true") on a session-authenticated document-download endpoint. originPatterns="*" combined with allowCredentials="true" makes Spring reflect the request's Origin header back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin while still allowing credentials, defeating the browser's same-origin protections. Any external website can issue a credentialed cross-origin request to /documents/{id} and read back a user's KYC documents if the session cookie is sent.

redeemCase() only calls auth.require(jwt.getSubject()) -- it never checks the caller's role (unlike every other compliance-facing endpoint, which gates on az.role(...,"compliance_officer")). Any authenticated user, including a plain 'prospect'/'customer' applicant, can call POST /api/rek-kyc/cases/redeem and -- given a valid caseRef envelope -- retrieve another customer's re-KYC case id and status with no ownership or role check at all.

shared() decrypts the caller-supplied 'c' parameter with seals.open(c) and returns a distinguishable HTTP status depending on the failure mode: BadPaddingException -> 403 FORBIDDEN ('Seal rejected') vs any other RuntimeException -> 422 UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY ('Seal content invalid'). Since the underlying cipher is unauthenticated AES/CBC (see CaseEnvelope/ReportSeal), this status-code oracle lets an attacker run a classic Vaudenay padding-oracle attack to decrypt or forge sealed scope tokens without knowing the key -- the same pattern repeats in redeemCase() at line 139.

seal()/open() use AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding with new IvParameterSpec(key) -- the IV is set to the exact same 16 bytes as the encryption key. Every message encrypted under this key uses the identical, fully predictable IV, which breaks CBC's semantic-security guarantee (identical plaintext prefixes produce identical ciphertext prefixes) and, combined with the lack of a MAC, makes the scheme vulnerable to chosen-ciphertext manipulation.

extra.message: legacySignIn() authenticates users by computing DigestUtils.md5Hex(passphrase) and comparing it to the stored legacyDigest. MD5 is cryptographically broken and unsalted here, making stored digests trivially crackable via rainbow tables/brute force if the user table is ever exposed, unlike the bcrypt-protected primary password path used elsewhere in this same class.

The web module's SecurityFilterChain explicitly disables frame protection: h.headers(x->x.frameOptions(fo->fo.disable())). This removes the X-Frame-Options header from every response, allowing the entire authenticated web UI (including state-changing forms like staff decisions, workforce suspension, and roster import) to be embedded in a hidden iframe on an attacker's page for clickjacking/UI-redress attacks.

cwe: CWE-1021: Improper Restriction of Rendered UI Layers or Frames

extra.message: verify() sends the provider API key as a plaintext URL query parameter over an unencrypted http:// connection: rest.postForObject("http://income-registry.internal/v1/statements/"+applicationId+"?apiKey="+key, ...). Query strings are commonly captured in server access logs, proxy logs, and browser history equivalents, and cleartext HTTP exposes the key to any network-level observer -- unlike DocumentCheckClient/CaseNarrationClient which pass the equivalent key in a header.

cwe: CWE-598: Use of GET Request Method With Sensitive Query Strings

Anyone who reads this source file obtains working admin credentials; per this codebase's own standard, seed/demo status does not excuse a disclosed credential from being a real finding.
